    <at_a_glance>
      <block>
        <text>The leaf stalk is almost missing. On most palms there is an obvious length of stem between the trunk and the leafy part of the frond; here it can be only an inch or two, so the enormous leaves seem to start almost directly at the crownshaft.</text>
      </block>

      <block>
        <text>This can become a genuinely big palm. In its home forests it can approach 100 feet tall, with individual fronds stretching to about fifteen feet.</text>
      </block>

        <text>“Gap” is not a made-up garden name. It is one of the local names recorded for this palm in New Guinea, along with many others spoken across its huge native range.</text>
      </block>

        <text>People have made remarkable use of it. The trunks and leaves have gone into house posts, floors, water pipes, roofing and even mattresses, and the growing palm heart has traditionally been eaten fresh or cooked.</text>

events.summary: Full page drafted from the editor's pasted XML, verified against Palmpedia and the Kew monograph. The unverified uses list (floors, water pipes, mattresses, palm heart) was cut — sources confirm construction use generally but not that specific list at species level. The conservation status claim was also removed: the IUCN 'Data Deficient' rating applies to the synonymised C. kisu under a narrower range, and the species' current status is not clearly resolved.
